source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, van Steenkiste, Linzen (2024) A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models
finding: PaLM 2 models reason more accurately than humans on syllogisms with a valid conclusion, but still make human-like errors (variable order effect, fallacies). Bigger models are more accurate.
numbers: 64 syllogism types; 27 have a valid conclusion other than 'nothing follows'. Human accuracy about 50% over those. Two largest PaLM 2 models above humans. Best LM about 75%. Zero-shot chain of thought prompt, 30 samples at temperature 0.5.
limits: Scale gives accuracy but not monotonically; the largest model was a little below the second largest. An earlier arXiv version had a sampling bug and different numbers.
agent_relevance: Accuracy and human-likeness come apart. A scaffold aimed at correctness should not copy human error patterns.

source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, van Steenkiste, Linzen (2024) A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models
finding: LMs almost never say 'nothing follows', which is the counterexample-driven answer. Humans are also reluctant, but LMs far more.
numbers: 'Nothing follows' is correct for 37 of 64 syllogisms. LM accuracy on those is close to 0%.
quote: the LMs' aversion to this response is much stronger than humans'
limits: Worst under the zero-shot CoT prompt used; the paper gives a separate elicitation paradigm in its appendix B.3 and leaves analysis to future work.
agent_relevance: This is the exact failure of the counterexample strategy: no search for a falsifying model, so a conclusion is accepted. An explicit forced search step for 'does a counterexample exist' targets it.

source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, van Steenkiste, Linzen (2024) A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models
finding: The mReasoner mental-model simulator has a System 2 knob (SYSTM2) that is the probability of searching for a counterexample. Fitting LM behavior to it shows larger models behave like high-SYSTM2, high-WEAKEN reasoners.
numbers: 1296 mReasoner parameter settings (LEN, BROAD, SYSTM2, WEAKEN), 923 finished; PC1 captures 77% of behavioral variance. With correct answers zeroed out as a control, PC1 still correlates 0.6 with SYSTM2 and 0 with accuracy.
limits: Interpretation depends on mReasoner being a good model of human behavior. Behavior fit is not proof of an internal counterexample search.
agent_relevance: A computational system built on this subfield: counterexample search is a tunable propensity. Suggests measuring our agent's own counterexample propensity and tuning it by signal (G1).

source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, van Steenkiste, Linzen (2024) A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models
finding: Counterexample search in mReasoner works by three moves: add an entity, move a property between entities, split one entity in two. If search is not triggered the reasoner accepts the first conclusion.
numbers: Three search moves described in section 5 and appendix figure 16.
limits: Applies to quantified syllogisms only.
agent_relevance: A ready-made operator set for a falsification step: add, move, split. Could be written as code-checked model-building moves.

source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, van Steenkiste, Linzen (2024) A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models
finding: LLaMA 2 models match human accuracy overall but fail syllogisms humans find easy (e.g. some A are B, all B are C), unlike PaLM 2. They do show the human variable-order effect.
numbers: Qualitative in the main text; plots in appendix E.
limits: Different model families disagree, so findings do not transfer by default.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a strategy profile measured on one model holds for another.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt, Bernardi (2024) A Systematic Analysis of Large Language Models as Soft Reasoners: The Case of Syllogistic Inferences
finding: Pre-trained LLMs use a form heuristic. The Atmosphere heuristic (conclusion mood copies premise quantifiers) predicts LLaMA-3 8B zero-shot-CoT outputs very well and may explain why it rarely says 'nothing follows'.
numbers: Atmosphere theory predicts 92% of LLaMA ZS-CoT correct valid conclusions, 82.97% of its errors on invalid schemas and 62.79% on valid schemas. Humans: 44.63% on valid, 40.97% on invalid. LLaMA-3 8B instruct reaches 50.00 overall; invalid-schema accuracy never reaches human level (best 32.50, LLaMA-3 70B instruct).
limits: Atmosphere is a fit to outputs, not proof of mechanism. Pseudo-word and believable-content conditions differ.
agent_relevance: The model's default is a cheap heuristic strategy, analogous to the statistical strategy in role. Invalid items need a counterexample step that the model skips unprompted.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt, Bernardi (2024) A Systematic Analysis of Large Language Models as Soft Reasoners: The Case of Syllogistic Inferences
finding: Prompting and training change the strategy. In-context examples and supervised fine-tuning raise accuracy on valid inferences; only fine-tuning removes most reasoning biases without harming consistency.
numbers: Zero-shot CoT accuracy falls as premises grow (2 to 3 to 4 premises). Instruction tuning helps invalid schemas but lowers valid-schema accuracy. Fine-tuned models reach about 93 to 99 on trained sets.
limits: Fine-tuned Pythia becomes inconsistent at the price of accuracy and struggles with unseen premise counts.
agent_relevance: Prompts alone give limited strategy control. Fits G11 (CoT is not free). A scaffold must test on held-out structure (G3), because fitted schemas do not generalise to length.

source: Holliday, Mandelkern, Zhang (2024) Conditional and Modal Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Twenty-nine LLMs all make basic mistakes with conditionals and modals. No model passes 90% on uncontroversial patterns (modus ponens, modus tollens, affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent and others). Larger models do better.
numbers: 29 models, temperature 0, 50% is guessing. Best: Llama 3.1 405B 89.50%; GPT-4 Turbo 87.17; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 85.33; Claude 3 Haiku 65.50. No model above 90%.
limits: The 'is this form of argument logically valid' wording lowered fallacy acceptance in some models.
agent_relevance: The conditional fallacies (AC, DA) are the signature of a no-counterexample-search strategy. Baseline for any strategy scaffold.

source: Holliday, Mandelkern, Zhang (2024) Conditional and Modal Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Zero-shot chain of thought reduces mistakes on conditional inference; few-shot does not reliably help.
numbers: Few-shot change versus zero-shot not significant (paired t-test). CoT gains in points: Claude 3 Haiku +21.5, GPT-4o mini +15.83, GPT-4o +13.5, Claude 3 Opus +13.5, Llama 3.1 405B about +4.3, Mistral Large 2 about +0.2. Few-shot: Gemini 1.5 Flash +10.67, Claude 3 Haiku +12.5, Mistral Large 2 -7.83.
limits: Column reading from extracted PDF text; weaker models gain most, strong models gain little. Prompt verb ('infer', 'deduce', 'conclude') mattered little (correlation over .9).
agent_relevance: Deliberate reasoning helps most where the model is weakest; for strong models extra reasoning gains little. Supports G12 (spend by difficulty).

source: Holliday, Mandelkern, Zhang (2024) Conditional and Modal Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: LLMs agree with human judgment in rejecting two inferences the material conditional would accept: contraposition (CT) and strengthening the antecedent (AS). So models do not treat 'if' as material.
numbers: Both patterns are rejected by most models, matching human intuition (appendix C.1.10 and C.1.11).
quote: LLMs, like ordinary human speakers, do not interpret the natural language conditional 'if. . . then' as a material conditional.
limits: Agreement in verdict does not show the same process. Models still show logically inconsistent judgments across modal and conditional patterns.
agent_relevance: Counterexample-style rejection of defeasible inferences is within reach; the weakness is consistency across patterns. Add a consistency check across paraphrases in code.

source: Kamath, Madathil, Schuster, de Marneffe, Reddy (2026) Humans and LLMs Diverge on Probabilistic Inferences (ProbCOPA)
finding: On graded probabilistic inferences, eight reasoning LLMs match humans only at the extremes (clearly likely or clearly unlikely). They avoid mid-scale answers and show far less variation than humans.
numbers: 210 items, 25 to 30 human raters each; 30 samples per item per model, verbalized 0 to 100 likelihood. Human split-half Spearman 0.98 and 0.97 across rounds. Model-human Wasserstein distances far larger than human-human; ensembling shrinks the gap but not to human level.
limits: Open-ended commonsense inferences, not the Markovits 90% versus 50% diagnostic items. Models include GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini-3, Kimi-K2, Qwen3, GLM-4.6.
agent_relevance: This is the statistical strategy side. Models are poor at calibrated middling probability; do not trust a verbalized probability from the model (consistent with G5, code normalises).

source: Kamath, Madathil, Schuster, de Marneffe, Reddy (2026) Humans and LLMs Diverge on Probabilistic Inferences (ProbCOPA)
finding: Temperature, persona prompts and more reasoning effort do not restore human-level variation or change model likelihood scores much.
numbers: Follow-up on the same 30 items as the human baseline: raising temperature did not reach human entropy before output turned to random tokens; persona prompting had limited effect; the reasoning effort setting did not significantly change scores.
limits: Small follow-up sample (30 items).
agent_relevance: Strategy cannot be changed by simple prompt knobs here. Supports G4: personas and temperature are not independent voters.

source: Kamath, Madathil, Schuster, de Marneffe, Reddy (2026) Humans and LLMs Diverge on Probabilistic Inferences (ProbCOPA)
finding: Reasoning chains show an alternatives-based pattern: models list other scenarios, then give a likelihood. Chain length grows with human disagreement.
numbers: 90 of 100 sampled chains explicitly weigh alternative scenarios. Spearman between chain length and human differential entropy: 0.50 for GLM-4.6 (p 2.1e-14), 0.30 to 0.36 for GPT-5 and Kimi-K2, 0.33 for the ensemble; weaker with human response time (about 0.12 to 0.25).
quote: 90 out of the 100 reasoning chains sampled include explicit considerations of alternative scenarios
limits: Manual inspection of 100 chains; faithfulness of chains is questioned by the authors themselves.
agent_relevance: Models already run a counterexample-flavored 'alternatives' routine inside probabilistic judgment: the two strategies blend. Length as a difficulty signal could drive budget allocation (G12), but chain text is not evidence (G10).

source: Orth, Mondorf, Plank (2026) If Probable, Then Acceptable? Understanding Conditional Acceptability Judgments in LLMs
finding: Llama and Qwen models are sensitive to conditional probability P(B|A) and to semantic relevance of A to B in acceptability ratings, but less consistently than humans. Bigger is not closer to humans.
numbers: Models: Llama 8B/70B, Qwen 7B/72B; vanilla, three-shot, and CoT (larger models only); compared with human data from Skovgaard-Olsen et al. (2016). Linear mixed models; probability effect significant (p<0.001) for vanilla models, slope up to 0.65 per unit of P(B|A) for one model; relevance effects vary and are weakest around 0.21 in one model.
limits: Only four open model families; human data not collected by the authors.
agent_relevance: Probability and relevance are separable cues in models too; the 'statistical' route is partly present in LLMs. Few-shot raised sensitivity; CoT effects mixed.

source: Wilie, Cahyawijaya, Ishii, He, Fung (2024) Belief Revision: The Adaptability of Large Language Models Reasoning (Belief-R)
finding: Built on the suppression task (Byrne 1989): an added premise should block a prior modus ponens conclusion. 30 LMs mostly fail to revise. Models good at updating are bad at keeping valid conclusions when no update is needed.
numbers: 30 LMs. Basic inference accuracy over 75% for pre-trained models above 6B parameters; instruction-tuned reach it at 2.7B. Most open models near 0% on belief-update accuracy; best reach at most 50% on the combined BREU score. Modus tollens harder than modus ponens.
limits: Logical-inference belief revision only (MP and MT). Not the Markovits item types, but the suppression task is the standard counterexample-availability paradigm.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that models do not spontaneously consider disabling conditions. A defeater-search step must be triggered by code, with a keep-or-update check to avoid over-updating (G1).

source: Wilie, Cahyawijaya, Ishii, He, Fung (2024) Belief Revision: The Adaptability of Large Language Models Reasoning (Belief-R)
finding: Better prompting does not fix belief revision. CoT gave no significant gain; Plan-and-Solve gave about 1 point of BREU.
numbers: Prompt variants tested: direct, CoT, Plan-and-Solve (PS); gain from PS about 1% BREU.
limits: Authors suspect missing-step errors; they did not test counterexample-specific prompts.
agent_relevance: Evidence against 'just ask for step-by-step' as the way to get counterexample strategy. Supports G2: tie revisions to real output.

source: Kirkpatrick, Sterken (2025) Generics and Default Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: On 20 defeasible reasoning patterns with generics (Birds fly), chain of thought often hurts. Many models treat generics as universals or fail to separate defeasible from deductive inference.
numbers: 28 LLMs, 20 patterns; for models above 75% zero-shot accuracy, CoT mean drop 11.14 points (SD 15.74), temperature 0. Few-shot helps modestly for some.
limits: Yes/no format; accuracy by pattern varies widely. Top zero-shot averages about 96%.
agent_relevance: Second case where CoT lowers accuracy on exception-tolerant inference. Do not apply a counterexample-hunting CoT by default (G1, G11); gate it.

source: Sinha, Goel, Kumaraguru, Geiping, Bethge, Prabhu (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? Evaluating Algorithmic Reasoning with Counterexample Creation (REFUTE)
finding: Finding a falsifying input for a subtly wrong solution is much harder than solving the problem. The best agent finds counterexamples for under 9% of wrong submissions.
numbers: o3-mini (high) with code-execution feedback: <9% of incorrect solutions falsified, though its ratings suggest it solves up to 48% of such problems. Success is not predicted by problem difficulty, author expertise or tests passed; on the subset that passes all initial tests success is 4% (+-1%).
limits: Algorithmic competition code; human experts had succeeded on every item. Counterexample is checkable by execution.
agent_relevance: Core boundary: counterexample strategy is expensive for models and weak. Plan for a high miss rate; a pass from 'no counterexample found' is never proof (G3).

source: Sinha, Goel, Kumaraguru, Geiping, Bethge, Prabhu (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? Evaluating Algorithmic Reasoning with Counterexample Creation (REFUTE)
finding: Explicitly prompting a search strategy (random generator plus brute force) did not help reasoning models; gains were marginal for chat models.
numbers: RandSearch success: DeepSeek-V3 4.0, Gemini Flash 2.0 Thinking 3.7, DeepSeek-R1 4.0, o3-mini (high) 8.3. With the correct solution handed over (Oracle): 15.1, 7.7, 9.9. 35% of RandSearch samples end in an incorrect counterexample; of these 86% come from wrong brute-force code, 14% from test validation errors. Search found 6% distinct new submissions for o3-mini versus 3% added by the oracle.
limits: Models rarely used a search strategy on their own, per manual inspection.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to choose the search strategy often hurts. Better: code owns the search loop, the model writes only small parts, and code validates them (program decides).

source: Drucker, Mahowald (2026) The Counterexample Game: Iterated Conceptual Analysis and Repair in Language Models
finding: An agent loop of counterexample then repair on definitions of 20 concepts hits diminishing returns quickly. Validity of model counterexamples falls over iterations; definitions grow without becoming more accurate.
numbers: Counterexamples valid: 69% at position 0, 42 to 50% at positions 1 and 2, 17 to 30% by positions 5 to 9. Chain-wide validity 36% Opus self-play versus 21% mixed-model. Definition length 11 to 95 words; accuracy plateaus after iteration 2. Full history did not help: 35.0% vs 36.0% validity (self-play), 16.7% vs 18.0% (mixed).
limits: Conceptual analysis, not deduction; judged by an LM judge (Opus 4.5) plus 5 humans on 60 items.
agent_relevance: A real counterexample-loop inside an LLM pipeline. Supports a hard cap on rounds and stopping when new counterexamples stop being valid (G1, G6, G11).

source: Drucker, Mahowald (2026) The Counterexample Game: Iterated Conceptual Analysis and Repair in Language Models
finding: An LM judge accepts about twice as many counterexamples as humans do, but agrees with humans above chance on which ones are good.
numbers: 60 items: 5 humans judged 32% valid on average, Opus 4.5 judged 60%. Of 108 human-Opus disagreements, 96 were human rejects and Opus accepts, 12 the reverse. Human-consensus vs Opus Cohen kappa 0.42 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.59); human-human kappa from 0.10 to 0.38.
limits: Small human sample; raters were not experts for every concept.
agent_relevance: A model judging counterexample validity is lenient (G5, G8): keep validity checks outside the model where possible.

source: Ravishankara (2025) FVA-RAG: Falsification-Verification Alignment for Mitigating Sycophantic Hallucinations
finding: A falsification loop inside a RAG agent: draft an answer, generate queries designed to find counter-evidence, then a verifier decides whether to overturn the draft.
numbers: TruthfulQA-Generation (817 queries): FVA-RAG 79.80 to 80.05% vs Self-RAG 71.11 to 72.22% and CRAG 71.36 to 73.93%. Falsification triggered on 24.5% (200/817) of queries, 29.3% with an evidence-enriched corpus.
limits: Single independent author, preprint, one benchmark; the verifier is itself a model. Treat as unreplicated.
agent_relevance: A method from this subfield (search for a falsifying case) inside an agent loop, with a trigger rate well under 100% (matches G1). Needs replication before we rely on it.

source: Li, Kuang, Huang, Xu et al. (2025) One Example Shown, Many Concepts Known! Counterexample-Driven Conceptual Reasoning in Mathematical LLMs (CounterMATH)
finding: On 1,216 textbook statements to prove or disprove by counterexample, most math-tuned open models score around 30 F1. Strong reasoning models do far better.
numbers: 1,216 pairs; about 87.8% of statements true, so macro F1 is used. Deepseek-R1 F1 80.7; Qwen2.5-Math-72B-Instruct 41.8; most 7B open models near 30 (e.g. Deepseek-Math-7B-rl 32.2). Open models often judge right without giving a valid example.
limits: Row alignment of the commercial-model table is garbled in text extraction; only R1 at 80.7 and Qwen-72B at 41.8 are stated in prose.
agent_relevance: Models may follow drill-learned procedures instead of exemplification. Check whether our agent actually produces a witness example.

source: Li, Kuang, Huang, Xu et al. (2025) One Example Shown, Many Concepts Known! Counterexample-Driven Conceptual Reasoning in Mathematical LLMs (CounterMATH)
finding: Training on only 1,025 counterexample-style examples gives a small gain on the benchmark and transfers to general math benchmarks. A hint prompt to reason by example helps little.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct: F1 38.3 base, about 39 with hint prompt, 41.1 fine-tuned (table row labels partly garbled). Out-of-distribution: MATH 80.5 to 87.9, AIME 2024 20.0 to 30.0, GSM8K 95.1 to 95.6.
limits: Small SFT set; discrepancies on some metrics acknowledged by the authors. Row labels uncertain in extraction.
agent_relevance: The counterexample habit can be trained, but a prompt hint barely changes behavior; our agent has no training, so rely on code-enforced steps.

source: Wang, Shi (2025) Logical forms complement probability in understanding language model (and human) performance
finding: Model accuracy on propositional and modal syllogisms depends on logical form as well as on input probability (perplexity). Modus tollens is the hardest form for most open models.
numbers: Soft accuracy (probability of Yes/No tokens) for 10 open models; e.g. llama-3-70b 0.714, mistral-8x7b 0.724, llama-2-7b 0.335. Reference runs: OpenAI-o1 0.926, Gemini-1.5-Pro 0.859, human 0.595. Possibility questions easier than necessity; shared argument-form preferences between humans and LLMs.
limits: Reference commercial runs use greedy decoding on 2,000 samples, not comparable with the probability-based scores. Human data from their own behavioral experiment.
agent_relevance: Modus tollens is the item class where counterexample reasoning is needed; models, like people, fare worst there. Use form-specific checks.

source: Dettki, Wu, Rehder (2026) Do LLMs Share Human-Like Biases? Causal Reasoning under Prior Knowledge, Irrelevant Context, and Varying Compute Budgets
finding: On collider causal judgments (11 tasks, 20+ LLMs), models use more rule-like strategies than humans and do not reproduce the human biases of weak explaining away and Markov violations.
numbers: 20+ LLMs against a matched human baseline; most LLMs show strong explaining away where humans show a weak effect. CoT improves alignment with human judgments up to a ceiling and increases robustness to irrelevant text.
limits: Workshop paper; causal judgment, not deduction.
agent_relevance: Models lean to the rule-based end of a rule versus probability split. Our agent may be more rule-like than a human by default; the statistical strategy has to be added deliberately where uncertainty is intrinsic.

source: Azin, Yu, Singh, Jouravlev (2026) Presupposition and Reasoning in Conditionals: A Theory-Based Study of Humans and LLMs
finding: With 120 humans and four LLMs on conditional presupposition, models that match human ratings best often lack coherent pragmatic reasoning when checked against a 59-question checklist.
numbers: 59-item checklist scored by an LLM judge (judge exact-match accuracy 89%, agreement 79.46% as stated); total checklist compliance about 60% for the strongest models and about 40% for open-source ones.
limits: LLM-as-judge checklist; sensitive to verbalization of reasoning.
agent_relevance: Output match with humans can hide a different process: do not use human-likeness of answers as a quality signal (G10).

source: Gomez-Sanchez et al. (2021) Conditional content, explicit information and generating cases: Sources for suppressing inferences
finding: Human baseline seen in search snippet only: prompting people to generate counterexamples increases suppression of conditional inferences. Effect larger in the counterexample-generation condition.
numbers: Two experiments per snippet; no figures read.
limits: Not opened; snippet only.
agent_relevance: Human evidence that asking for counterexamples shifts strategy deliberately, the test to run on LLMs next.

source: Lean Disprove: Certified Counterexample Search for AI-Assisted Formal Mathematics (ICML 2026 listing)
finding: A bounded cycle that searches for certified counterexamples to Lean goals using enumeration, random sampling and SAT/SMT queries.
numbers: None read.
limits: Listing only; not opened.
agent_relevance: Shows the counterexample step can be handed to a solver with a certificate, which fits our rule that code, not the model, checks.

source: Search gap: no study found that runs Markovits-style strategy diagnostic items (90% vs 50% probability cues, time pressure) on language models
finding: Across web and OpenAlex searches, no direct LLM test of the dual-strategy diagnostic was found as of 2026-10-21.
numbers: Queries: counterexample/statistical strategy LLM; suppression effect LLM; PHM vs mental models LLM; counterexample loop agent. Closest: mReasoner mapping in Eisape et al. and ProbCOPA.
limits: Absence in a few searches, not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Open question and an original experiment: run diagnostic items on our agent with and without a forced counterexample step, and with token budget as the analog of time pressure.
